title: DNA, Proteins & Cell Division (Extended)
description: DNA structure and base pairing, how genes code for proteins through mRNA and ribosomes, haploid and diploid cells, and mitosis versus meiosis — the Extended tier of IGCSE Biology 0610.

notes.heading: The Structure of DNA
notes.body:
📌 Definition
A **DNA** molecule is made of **two strands coiled around each other** — the **double helix**. Each strand contains a series of **bases**, and **bonds between the base pairs hold the two strands together**.

🔑 The base-pairing rule (learn it as two pairs)
• **A pairs with T**
• **C pairs with G**
Only the letters are needed — the full names of the bases are not required.

🔑 What the examiner wants
Three separately creditable facts: (1) two strands, (2) coiled into a double helix, (3) bases paired A–T and C–G, with the bonds between the pairs holding the strands together. A diagram question may ask you to label a strand, a base and a bond.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Pairing A with G or C with T. There is no trick here — learn **A–T** and **C–G** as two fixed units and write them first in any DNA question.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Double helix = two coiled strands held together by bonds between base pairs.
• A with T; C with G.

illustration.alt: A DNA ladder diagram showing two strands joined by paired bases: A pairs with T and C pairs with G, with bonds between the base pairs holding the strands together.
illustration.caption: Two strands coiled into a double helix; the A–T and C–G base pairs bond the strands together.

notes.heading: From Gene to Protein: Why the Base Sequence Matters
notes.body:
📌 The key idea
The **sequence of bases in a gene codes for the sequence of amino acids in a protein**. Change the base sequence and you change the protein the gene produces.

🔑 Why the sequence matters
• Proteins are long chains of amino acids that fold into precise three-dimensional shapes.
• **Different amino acid sequences give proteins different shapes** — and the shape decides what the protein can do. For an enzyme, the shape of the active site decides which substrate it can bind.

🔑 How DNA controls a cell
**DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of proteins**. The syllabus names three kinds:
• **enzymes** — control the cell's chemical reactions,
• **membrane carriers** — control which substances enter and leave the cell,
• **neurotransmitter receptors** — let cells respond to signals from nerve cells.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that DNA 'makes characteristics' directly. The chain is always: gene (base sequence) → protein (amino acid sequence → shape) → cell function.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Base sequence → amino acid sequence → protein shape → protein function.
• DNA controls cells through proteins: enzymes, membrane carriers and neurotransmitter receptors.

notes.heading: How a Protein Is Made — and Why Cells Differ
notes.body:
🔑 The sequence of events (learn the ORDER — sequencing questions are common)
1. The **gene stays in the nucleus** — the DNA itself never leaves it.
2. A copy of the gene is made in the nucleus: a molecule of **messenger RNA (mRNA)**.
3. The mRNA **moves out into the cytoplasm**.
4. The mRNA **passes through ribosomes**.
5. The ribosome **assembles amino acids into a protein**, in the order set by the **sequence of bases in the mRNA**.

🔑 Same genes, different cells
Almost every body cell contains the **same set of genes**, but **many of those genes are not expressed**. A cell makes only the proteins it needs — a muscle cell makes contractile proteins, a pancreas cell makes digestive enzymes. That is how genetically identical cells end up as different tissues.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing that DNA travels to the ribosome. Only the mRNA COPY leaves the nucleus; the gene itself stays in the nucleus.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Gene (stays in nucleus) → mRNA copy → cytoplasm → ribosome → protein.
• Cells differ because different genes are expressed, not because they carry different genes.

notes.heading: Haploid and Diploid
notes.body:
📌 Definitions
• A **haploid nucleus** contains a **single set of unpaired chromosomes** — gametes (sperm and egg cells) are haploid.
• A **diploid nucleus** contains **two sets of chromosomes**, held as **pairs** — normal body cells are diploid.
• A human diploid cell has **46 chromosomes = 23 pairs**; a human gamete has **23 single chromosomes**.

🔑 Why the pairing matters
One chromosome of each pair came from the mother and one from the father — so each parent contributes one allele of every gene.

💡 Worked Example
Sperm (23 chromosomes) + egg (23 chromosomes) → zygote (46 chromosomes, 23 pairs). Gametes MUST be haploid, otherwise the chromosome number would double in every generation.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Writing '46 pairs'. A human diploid cell has 46 chromosomes arranged in 23 PAIRS — 92 chromosomes would be a cell that has replicated its DNA, not a normal body cell.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Haploid = one set (23 in humans); diploid = two sets (46, as 23 pairs).
• Gametes are haploid; body cells are diploid.

notes.heading: Mitosis
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Mitosis** is a nuclear division that produces **two daughter cells genetically identical** to each other and to the parent cell. (The stages of mitosis are not required.)

🔑 How the chromosome number is maintained
• BEFORE the division, **exact copies of every chromosome are made** (replication).
• The two copies of each chromosome then **separate**, one copy into each daughter nucleus — so the chromosome number stays the same (46 → 46 in humans).

🔑 The four roles (a frequent 4-mark list)
• **Growth** of the organism.
• **Repair** of damaged tissues.
• **Replacement** of worn-out or dying cells (e.g. skin and blood cells).
• **Asexual reproduction** — offspring from one parent are genetically identical clones.

📌 Stem cells
**Stem cells** are **unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis** and can then **become specialised** into different cell types — e.g. bone marrow stem cells producing red and white blood cells.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying the chromosomes are 'halved' before mitosis — that describes meiosis. In mitosis the chromosomes are COPIED and the copies are shared equally.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Mitosis: copy the chromosomes → separate the copies → two identical diploid cells.
• Roles: growth, repair, replacement, asexual reproduction; stem cells divide by mitosis.

notes.heading: Meiosis
notes.body:
📌 Definition
**Meiosis** is a nuclear division involved in the **production of gametes** (sperm and egg cells). (No stage detail is required.)

🔑 Reduction division
• Meiosis is a **reduction division**: the chromosome number is **halved from diploid to haploid** (46 → 23 in humans).
• The haploid gametes can then fuse at fertilisation and restore the diploid number in the zygote.

🔑 Genetically different cells
• Unlike mitosis, meiosis produces cells that are **genetically different from each other** and from the parent cell.
• This shuffling of alleles is a major source of the **variation** on which natural selection acts — the link back to the Inheritance & Variation topic.

💡 Worked Example
A human ovary cell (diploid, 46 chromosomes) undergoes meiosis → egg cells (haploid, 23 chromosomes), each carrying a different combination of the parent's alleles.

⚠️ Common Mistake
Saying gametes are produced by mitosis. Mitosis makes identical body cells; only meiosis makes the haploid, genetically different gametes.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Meiosis = gamete production; diploid → haploid (reduction division).
• The products are genetically different — a source of variation.

notes.heading: Mitosis vs Meiosis — Answer 'Compare' Questions in Pairs
notes.body:
🔑 The comparison table
• **Purpose** — mitosis: growth, repair, replacement and asexual reproduction / meiosis: production of gametes.
• **Chromosome number** — mitosis: maintained (diploid → diploid) / meiosis: halved (diploid → haploid).
• **Genetic outcome** — mitosis: daughter cells genetically identical / meiosis: cells genetically different.
• **Where** — mitosis: throughout the body / meiosis: in the reproductive organs.

🔑 What the examiner wants
In a 'compare' or 'describe the differences' question, make PAIRED statements about the same feature: 'mitosis keeps the chromosome number constant, whereas meiosis halves it'. Two separate one-sided sentences about different features often score only half the marks.

💡 Worked Example
'A skin cell divides by mitosis so the two new cells each have 46 chromosomes identical to the parent cell; a cell in the testis divides by meiosis so the sperm produced have 23 chromosomes and are genetically different from one another.'

⚠️ Common Mistake
Mixing the rows — e.g. 'meiosis produces identical cells for growth'. If you learn the table as three paired rows, a muddled row stands out immediately.

📎 Key Points to Remember
• Same start (one diploid nucleus), different ends: identical diploid body cells vs different haploid gametes.
• Both are nuclear divisions; only meiosis is a reduction division.

flashcards.definition: The shape of a DNA molecule: two strands coiled around each other, held together by bonds between paired bases.
flashcards.example: The two strands of a DNA molecule twist around each other like a coiled ladder.

flashcards.definition: In DNA, base A always pairs with base T, and base C always pairs with base G; bonds between the base pairs hold the two strands together.
flashcards.example: If one strand reads A-T-C-G, the paired bases on the other strand are T-A-G-C.

flashcards.definition: A copy of a gene, made in the nucleus, which moves out into the cytoplasm and passes through ribosomes.
flashcards.example: The mRNA copy carries the gene's base sequence to the ribosome; the gene itself stays in the nucleus.

flashcards.definition: The cell structure that mRNA passes through and that assembles amino acids into a protein, in the order set by the mRNA base sequence.
flashcards.example: Ribosomes in a pancreas cell assemble amino acids into the enzyme amylase.

flashcards.definition: Most body cells contain the same genes, but many are not expressed — each cell makes only the proteins it needs.
flashcards.example: A muscle cell expresses genes for contractile proteins; a nerve cell does not.

flashcards.definition: A nucleus containing a single set of unpaired chromosomes.
flashcards.example: A human sperm cell is haploid: 23 single chromosomes.

flashcards.definition: A nucleus containing two sets of chromosomes, arranged as pairs.
flashcards.example: A human body cell is diploid: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs.

flashcards.definition: Nuclear division that produces two genetically identical daughter cells, maintaining the chromosome number.
flashcards.example: Skin cells divide by mitosis to replace worn-out cells.

flashcards.definition: Nuclear division involved in gamete production, producing cells that are genetically different from each other.
flashcards.example: Cells in the testes divide by meiosis to form sperm.

flashcards.definition: The halving of the chromosome number from diploid to haploid during meiosis.
flashcards.example: A human cell with 46 chromosomes produces gametes with 23 chromosomes by reduction division.

flashcards.definition: An unspecialised cell that divides by mitosis and can become specialised into different cell types.
flashcards.example: Bone marrow stem cells produce red blood cells and white blood cells.

flashcards.definition: DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of proteins, including enzymes, membrane carriers and neurotransmitter receptors.
flashcards.example: By making a particular membrane carrier protein, a cell controls what enters and leaves.

questions.stem: In a DNA molecule, which base pairs with A?
choices: C
T
G
A
questions.explanation: The base-pairing rule is A with T and C with G. Pairing A with G or with itself would not fit the bonding pattern that holds the two strands together.

questions.stem: What holds the two strands of a DNA molecule together?
choices: Ribosomes gripping the strands
The nuclear membrane
Covalent bonds between amino acids
Bonds between the paired bases
questions.explanation: Bonds between the base pairs (A–T and C–G) hold the two strands together in the double helix. Amino acids build proteins, not DNA, and ribosomes are the site of protein assembly.

questions.stem: The sequence of bases in a gene determines:
choices: the sequence of amino acids in a protein
the number of chromosomes in the cell
the shape of the nucleus
the permeability of the cell membrane
questions.explanation: A gene's base sequence codes for the amino acid sequence of a protein; different amino acid sequences fold into different protein shapes with different functions. Chromosome number and nuclear shape are not set by a single gene's base sequence.

questions.stem: Which sequence correctly describes how a protein is made?
choices: A ribosome enters the nucleus → reads the gene → the protein is exported to the cytoplasm
DNA leaves the nucleus → ribosomes copy it → amino acids are assembled
An mRNA copy of the gene is made in the nucleus → the mRNA moves into the cytoplasm → it passes through ribosomes → the ribosome assembles amino acids in the order set by the mRNA bases
Amino acids are assembled in the nucleus → DNA carries the finished protein to the ribosome
questions.explanation: The gene stays in the nucleus; an mRNA copy is made there, moves to the cytoplasm and passes through ribosomes, which assemble the amino acids in the mRNA's base-sequence order. DNA never leaves the nucleus and ribosomes do not enter it.

questions.stem: How many chromosomes are there in a human sperm cell?
questions.explanation: A sperm cell is a gamete with a haploid nucleus — a single set of 23 unpaired chromosomes. 46 is the diploid number of a body cell; 92 is neither.

choices: 23 unpaired chromosomes
46 chromosomes arranged as 23 pairs
46 pairs of chromosomes
a single set of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Diploid means two sets of chromosomes, held as pairs: 46 chromosomes in 23 pairs. '46 pairs' would be 92 chromosomes, and a single unpaired set describes a haploid gamete.

questions.stem: Which of these is NOT a role of mitosis?
choices: Growth of an organism
Repair of damaged tissue
Asexual reproduction
Production of gametes
questions.explanation: Gametes are produced by MEIOSIS, which halves the chromosome number. Mitosis — which produces genetically identical cells — is used for growth, repair, replacement of cells and asexual reproduction.

questions.stem: Why are the two daughter cells produced by mitosis genetically identical to the parent cell?
choices: The cell divides without copying its DNA, so nothing can change
The chromosomes are halved before division
Exact copies of every chromosome are made before division, and the copies separate so each daughter cell keeps the full chromosome number
The two daughter cells exchange alleles after division
questions.explanation: Before mitosis every chromosome is replicated exactly; the copies then separate into the two daughter nuclei, so each receives an identical, complete set — the chromosome number is maintained. Halving the chromosomes is what meiosis does.

questions.stem: What is the main role of meiosis?
choices: Producing haploid gametes for sexual reproduction
Growth of the embryo
Repairing skin wounds
Producing genetically identical clones
questions.explanation: Meiosis is the reduction division that produces haploid gametes (sperm and eggs). Growth, repair and cloning-type reproduction are all roles of mitosis, which keeps cells diploid and identical.

questions.stem: Offspring produced by sexual reproduction are genetically different from each other mainly because:
choices: mitosis halves the chromosome number
meiosis produces gametes that are genetically different, and fertilisation combines gametes from two different parents
mutations always happen at fertilisation
the offspring's body cells contain different genes from each other
questions.explanation: Two sources of difference stack up: meiosis produces gametes that are genetically different from one another, and each offspring results from a different pairing of one sperm and one egg from two parents. Mitosis does not halve chromosomes — that is meiosis.

questions.stem: Stem cells are best described as:
choices: cells that have lost their nucleus
fully specialised cells that can no longer divide
gametes formed by meiosis
unspecialised cells that divide by mitosis and can become specialised into different cell types
questions.explanation: Stem cells are unspecialised, divide by mitosis, and can then differentiate — e.g. bone marrow stem cells forming red and white blood cells. A cell without a nucleus (like a mature red blood cell) cannot divide at all.

questions.stem: A nerve cell and a muscle cell from the same person contain the same genes, yet they look and function very differently. Why?
choices: Each cell type has deleted the genes it does not need
Mutations occurred as the cells specialised
Many genes are not expressed — each cell makes only the proteins it needs
The two cell types contain different numbers of chromosomes
questions.explanation: Almost all body cells carry the same full set of genes, but each cell expresses only some of them — making only the proteins it needs. The genes are not deleted, and both cell types are diploid with 46 chromosomes.

questions.stem: DNA controls cell function by controlling the production of:
choices: proteins, such as enzymes, membrane carriers and neurotransmitter receptors
carbohydrates, such as starch and cellulose
lipids for the cell membrane
water and mineral ions
questions.explanation: Genes code for proteins, so DNA exerts control through protein production — the syllabus names enzymes, membrane carriers and neurotransmitter receptors. Carbohydrates and lipids are made by enzymes, not coded for directly.

questions.stem: A human skin cell divides by mitosis, and a cell in the testis divides by meiosis to form sperm. Which row of the table is correct?
choices: Mitosis daughter cells: 46 chromosomes, genetically different; sperm: 46 chromosomes, genetically identical
Mitosis daughter cells: 23 chromosomes, genetically identical; sperm: 46 chromosomes, genetically different
Mitosis daughter cells: 23 chromosomes, genetically different; sperm: 23 chromosomes, genetically identical
Mitosis daughter cells: 46 chromosomes, genetically identical; sperm: 23 chromosomes, genetically different
questions.explanation: Mitosis maintains the diploid number and gives identical cells (46, identical); meiosis is the reduction division giving genetically different haploid gametes (23, different). Any row mixing 23 with mitosis or 46 with sperm reverses the two processes.

questions.stem: Which statement correctly compares mitosis and meiosis?
choices: Mitosis halves the chromosome number; meiosis maintains it
Mitosis produces genetically identical cells, whereas meiosis produces genetically different cells
Both mitosis and meiosis produce gametes
Meiosis is used for tissue repair; mitosis is used to make gametes
questions.explanation: Mitosis → identical cells, chromosome number maintained, for growth/repair/replacement/asexual reproduction; meiosis → different cells, chromosome number halved, for gametes. The other statements swap or confuse the two processes.
